ety.text: From Middle English session, from Old French session, from Latin sessiō (“a sitting”), from sedeō (“sit”).

senses.d: A period of time devoted to a particular activity.

An official meeting or term of a council, court, or other body to conduct its business; e.g. the annual or semiannual periods of a legislature (that together comprise the legislative term), whose individual meetings are also called sessions.
ex: This court is now in session.

senses.d: The sequence of interactions between client and server, or between user and system; the period during which a user is logged in or connected.
ex: Logging out or shutting down the computer will end your session.

senses.d: Any of the three scheduled two-hour playing sessions, from the start of play to lunch, from lunch to tea and from tea to the close of play.
The act of sitting, or the state of being seated.
ex: So much his ascension into heaven and his session at the right hand of God do import.

senses.d: An academic term; semester; school year.
An extended period of drinking, typically consuming beer with low alcohol content.
The ruling body of a congregation, consisting of the pastor and elders.
To hold or participate in a jam session with other musicians.
ex: “I downloaded a clip from a drummer, who I now realize is Bernard Purdie, who has sessioned on all kinds of records,” he said.

From late Middle English sisamie, from Latin sīsamum, sēsamum, from Ancient Greek σήσαμον (sḗsamon), from Aramaic שושמא (šūššmā), shortening of שומשומא (šumššumā), from Akkadian 𒊭𒈦𒌑𒈬 (šamaššammū, “oil plant”), compound of 𒉌𒄑 (šaman, “oil”) and 𒌑 (šammum, “plant”). The modern pronunciation is perhaps influenced by (transliterations of) Greek σησάμη (sisámi). Doublet of sesamum.

senses.d: A tropical Asian plant (Sesamum indicum) bearing small flat seeds used as food and as a source of oil.

ety.text: Ultimately from Arabic جُلْجُلَان (juljulān, “sesame”) via a dialect. Sicilian giurgiulena.

Inherited from Old Spanish ajonjolí, aljonjolí, from an ambiguous Andalusian Arabic form, of raised final vowel from Arabic جُلْجُلَان (juljulān, “sesame seed”), or of clipped ending, جُلْجُل (juljul) + -í (nisba), as the descendants of the pomegranate cultivar سَفَرِيّ (safariyy), or rather + -ín (diminutive) in view…
